doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
title: The standard repertoire of the early 1940s
summary: He lists the tunes everyone had to know from Ellington, Lunceford, Waller, Erskine Hawkins, Basie and Pres.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: What was the repertoire? All the songs were coming from pop music, from Broadway plays and things like that?
Mostly. Duke Ellington and Jimmie Lunceford had some input.
Fats Waller. Then Erskine Hawkins had two or three numbers that you had to know. After Hours. Every piano player had to know After Hours.
Then he had Tuxedo Junction. Every trumpet player had to know it. [Freeman sings.] Everybody, even all the horn players, saxophone players, knew this solo.
Then you had certain riff tunes that you had to know, like a Flyin’ Home type thing.
That was the standard repertoire that you had to know to play, because Dizzy hadn’t really come on the scene with his tunes, nor had Bird.
What about things like Tickle Toe and stuff like that?
But you had to know that kind of stuff too?
Oh yeah. You had to know all the Pres that you could possibly find. Of course everything he played was at – except [?] . To me that’s one of his greatest tunes. That was kind of bright.
